exp.1:14:
Paul tells Titus to teach these things: to speak, encourage, and correct with firmness. "Exhort" means to encourage and call others to obey. "Rebuke" means to correct clearly. "With all authority" points to the authority of the truth he teaches, not to the authority of his personal character. "Let no man despise you" means he should not allow himself to be treated as someone unimportant.

Paul writes to Titus, his co-worker, who was guiding the churches in Crete. He has just reminded him that Jesus gave himself to redeem us and to form a people devoted to good works. For that reason, the teaching must lead to a transformed life. Some understand that Paul is encouraging Titus in the face of possible criticism; the text gives no further details.

For today: if you teach, counsel, or guide others, do so with firmness and with love, grounded in God's Word and not in your own opinion. And make sure your life supports what you say.
exp.2:13:
This verse says that believers should learn to devote themselves to good works, that is, to help with what is truly needed. Here "to be concerned" means to conduct oneself or to engage in good works with steadiness. "Necessary uses" are the real needs, such as those of Zenas and Apollos. The goal is that their faith not be "unfruitful," that is, barren.

Paul writes to Titus, who is in Crete, and closes his letter with practical instructions. He has just asked Titus to help Zenas and Apollos on their journey. In this way he shows the Christians of Crete a concrete way to do good. Some closing notes in the text, such as the mention of Nicopolis, are not part of the original letter and were added later.

For today: look for a specific need near you, such as a neighbor, a brother or sister in your church, or a missionary, and help them with steady commitment. A living faith shows itself in practical service.
exp.1:7:
Paul asks that Titus's words be sound, meaning solid, true and healthy, so that no one can rightly find fault with them. The goal is that the opponent of the faith will be put to shame when he finds nothing bad to say about believers.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he left in Crete to set the churches in order. He has already given instructions for older men, older women, and younger people. Here he reminds Titus that his teaching must go together with a consistent life, because outsiders watch Christians and judge the message by their conduct.

For today: make sure your words are true and respectful, including on social media, at work, and at home. Live and speak so honestly that, if anyone wants to criticize your faith, they cannot find a valid reason.
exp.1:5:
This verse says Titus should encourage and advise the young men to be "sober-minded." That word means prudent, sensible, self-controlled, people who think before they act. "Young men" refers to the young men, and "exhort" means to encourage firmly and with affection.

Paul writes this letter to Titus, who was caring for the churches on the island of Crete. He gives instructions for each group: older men, older women, young women, and now young men. The purpose, according to the context, is that faith be lived out in an orderly way and that no one speak evil of the word of God.

For today: before reacting in anger, spending money, or making an important decision, pause and pray. Mastering your impulses is a simple way to show the character of Christ.
exp.1:3:
This verse follows the previous instruction: older women are to teach the younger women. They teach them to be "sober," that is, sensible and self-controlled, and to love their husbands and their children.

Paul writes to Titus, who was overseeing the churches on the island of Crete. He wanted the lives of believers to show order and good witness, so that no one would speak badly of the word of God (v. 5). Here we see how wisdom was passed from one generation to the next within the church. Some understand these words according to the customs of that time; others see principles that still apply today.

Today we can seek relationships of mentoring between generations. If you are older, share humbly what you have learned; if you are younger, ask for advice from someone mature in the faith.
exp.0:6:
This verse says that the leader of the church, called here "bishop" (overseer or supervisor), must be blameless, that is, without a just accusation against his conduct. He is a "steward of God," that is, a manager of what belongs to God. He must not be selfwilled, nor quick to anger, nor given to wine, nor a striker, nor seek money in a dishonest way.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he left in Crete to set the church in order and appoint elders in every town. In this passage "elder" and "bishop" seem to refer to the same office, although some understand it differently. Paul wants leaders to have a trustworthy character.

For today: if you lead in your home, work, or church, examine your character. Ask God for help to control your anger, to be humble, and to handle money with honesty.
exp.2:4:
It says God saved us, but not because of good things we had done that earned it. He saved us because he is merciful. The words "washing" and "regeneration" from the older wording are rewritten here: the verse speaks of being washed and of being born again. "Renewing by the Holy Spirit" speaks of a life made new by the Spirit. Some Christians see here a reference to baptism; others see a spiritual cleansing that God brings about in the heart.

The apostle Paul writes to Titus, his co-worker, who was looking after the churches in Crete. Earlier, Paul recalls how we lived without God: lost, selfish, and full of resentment. Then he shows that the change came through the kindness of God, not through our effort. In this way Titus could teach with humility and without pride.

For today: if you feel unworthy, remember that God loves you because of his mercy, not because of your record. Rest in his grace, and treat others with the same patience you have received.
exp.1:0:
It says that Titus should teach what agrees with "sound doctrine," that is, the teaching that is healthy and true. The word "but" in the verse marks a contrast, and "becomes" means "is fitting" or "is appropriate." Paul asks Titus that his words fit with the gospel.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he left on the island of Crete to put the churches in order and appoint elders. Before this verse, Paul speaks of false teachers who lead people astray. By contrast, Titus must teach what is sound. The verses that follow show that this teaching shows itself in the daily life of both young and old.

Today, before we give opinions or advice to others, we can ask ourselves: "Does what I say agree with what the Bible teaches and with a life that honors God?" Let us speak with truth and with a good example.
exp.0:5:
This verse describes what a person must be like to be appointed as an elder in the church. He must be "blameless," that is, without reproach, with a good reputation. "The husband of one wife" is usually understood to mean faithful in his marriage, although some interpret it in other ways. His children must be believers and not accused of riot or unruly behavior.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he left on the island of Crete to set in order the churches and appoint elders in every town. Paul wanted the leaders to have a solid testimony, and the home was the first test of their character. How the part about the children is understood varies among Christians.

For today: before seeking a position or a place of influence, take care of your character at home. Be faithful, patient, and a good example to your family, for that is where what you truly are becomes visible.
exp.0:7:
This verse describes the positive qualities of a church leader. "Hospitable" is someone who opens their home gladly to others. "Loving what is good" loves what is right. "Self-controlled" knows how to restrain themselves. "Just" acts with righteousness. "Holy" lives devoted to God. "Self-restrained" means they master their desires and do not let themselves be carried away by them.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he left on the island of Crete to set things in order in the churches and to appoint leaders. Before this list, Paul mentioned what the leader must avoid, such as pride, anger, and greed. Here he shows the positive side. Afterward he explains that the leader must defend sound teaching, because there were false teachers confusing many people.

For today: it is not enough to avoid what is wrong; God calls us to cultivate what is good. This week, practice one of these qualities, for example by inviting someone to your table or by controlling an impulsive reaction.
exp.2:11:
Here Paul tells Titus that, when he sends Artemas or Tychicus to him, Titus should make every effort to come to see him at Nicopolis, because he has decided to spend the winter there. The sentence about the quoted source words is dropped, since neither word appears in the verse your reader sees.

Paul writes this letter to Titus, whom he left in charge of the churches on Crete. After giving him instructions about sound teaching and good order, he closes with practical matters. We do not know for certain which Nicopolis this was, although several cities had that name; many think of the one on the western coast of Greece. We also do not know who would have replaced Titus.

For today: faith is also lived out in the ordinary, such as planning, coordinating, and supporting others. Serve God with order and willingness, and help with practical needs without expecting recognition.
exp.1:2:
This verse speaks about the older women in the church. Paul asks them to live in a way that honors God, with conduct that is becoming of holiness, meaning a manner of living that fits those who belong to Him. They must not be false accusers, that is, people who speak badly of others. Nor are they to be given to much wine, enslaved by alcohol. And they are to be teachers of good things, which means teaching what is good and worthy.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he left on the island of Crete to set the churches in order. He wants the teaching to be accompanied by a consistent life. Each group, older men and older women, has a role. The older women prepare the way for them to teach the younger women, as the text goes on to say.

For today: if you are an older person, watch your words and your example, because the younger ones are watching you. If you are young, seek the counsel of mature believers.
exp.2:0:
It says that Titus should remind the believers to submit to rulers and authorities, to obey them, and to be ready to do good.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he left in charge of the church in Crete. He wants Christians to have an orderly life that adorns the gospel. The following verses call for avoiding insult and quarrelling, and remind readers that before, everyone lived without God and needed mercy. Some think that obedience has limits when authority demands sin, but this text does not address that directly.

For today: respect the laws and the authorities, such as paying taxes or following rules. Also, look for a concrete opportunity to serve your community, showing humility and kindness even when you do not agree.
exp.0:1:
Paul says that the faith and service of his ministry point toward the hope of eternal life. That life is not a human invention: God promised it, and God, who cannot lie, is incapable of failing to keep his word. The phrase "before the world began" speaks of something prior to human history. It can be understood as a plan settled from eternity, though some interpret it as a promise made in the most ancient times.

Paul introduces himself to Titus, his co-worker, at the start of the letter. He reminds him that his ministry exists to awaken faith and truth in God's chosen people, and that everything rests on a sure promise. Titus was to put order in the churches of Crete.

For today: when your hope wavers because of doubts or trials, base it on the character of God rather than on your feelings. If God does not lie, his promise is firm.
exp.0:4:
Paul reminds Titus why he left him on the island of Crete: so that he would put in order what was still incomplete or disorganized, and so that he would appoint elders (leaders of the church) in every town. Towns are small cities or settlements, and to put things in order means to set right what needs correcting.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he calls his true son in the common faith. It seems Titus was a trusted coworker. The churches in Crete were young and needed a healthy structure. That is why Paul gives him instructions, and in the verses that follow he explains what character these leaders should have. The terms "elder" and "overseer" appear here to refer to the same office, although some understand it differently.

For today: God cares for his church with order and with leaders of good character. Pray for your pastors and, if you serve in any way, make sure your life supports your words.
exp.0:10:
This verse says that certain people must be silenced, that is, prevented from continuing to teach. "Stopping their mouths" is a way of saying their arguments must be refuted so that they no longer keep speaking. They "upset whole households," meaning they throw families into disorder and harm them with teachings that are not correct. They do this "for dishonest gain," that is, for shameful profit, for money.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he left on the island of Crete to set in order the churches and appoint elders. Paul speaks of rebellious teachers, especially those of Jewish background, who took advantage of the people. For this reason he asks that Titus confront them with the truth and correct them.

Today we can examine what we hear by comparing it with the Bible. If anyone uses faith to enrich themselves or to divide families, we should be careful and seek wise counsel.
exp.1:11:
This verse says that God's grace teaches us to say "no" to two things: ungodliness, which is living without regard for God, and worldly desires, which are the longings that pull us away from Him. And it teaches us to live in three ways: with self-control, with righteousness toward others, and with reverence for God.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he left in Crete to put the churches in order. Earlier he has given instructions to older men, older women, young people, and slaves. Here he explains the reason behind all of it: God's grace saves and also transforms. A good life is not done to earn salvation, but to reflect it.

For today: think of one habit or desire that pulls you away from God, and ask God that His grace would help you change it this week, with one concrete step.
exp.2:12:
Paul asks Titus to help with the journey of Zenas and Apollos, and to make sure they have everything they need. The phrase "a lawyer" refers to an expert in the law; the verse does not say whether it meant Jewish law or Roman law, and scholars debate it. Paul's request to send them on their way means to see them off with provisions.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he left in Crete to set the churches in order. At the end of the letter he gives practical instructions. Zenas and Apollos seem to be passing through, and Paul wants Titus to welcome them well. We do not know with certainty where they were going. This Apollos is probably the same teacher who appears in Acts, although the text does not say so.

Today we can show our faith through concrete help. Think about who serves God near you, such as a pastor, a missionary or a teacher, and how you could support them with something practical: transportation, food, an offering or a word of encouragement.
exp.1:1:
This verse tells the older men how they should live. "Temperate" means they have self-control and do not give in to excess. "Grave" means serious and worthy of respect. "Prudent" describes those who think carefully before they act. "Sound in faith" means having a firm faith without error. "Charity" is love, and "patience" is steadiness through difficulties.

Paul writes to Titus, who was overseeing the churches on the island of Crete. He asks him to teach what agrees with sound doctrine, that is, teaching that is put into practice. Then he gives advice to the older women, the young people, and the servants. Christian faith was meant to be seen in the whole life of the community.

For today: if you are an older person, work at being an example of faith, love, and patience. If you are young, value and learn from those who have walked with God for many years.
exp.0:15:
Some people, the verse says, claim to know God, but their actions show the opposite. "They profess" in the verse means they declare it openly. It also notes that the words "abominable" and "reprobate" are not literally in the verse; the verse's wording "abominable" is what is used, and to be "reprobate" means to be unfit or worthless for doing good. Those who are "disobedient" are the ones who do not obey.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he left in Crete to put the churches in order. There were teachers there who followed Jewish myths and human rules. Paul says that their hearts and consciences were defiled, and so their lives contradicted their words. Scholars debate the details of exactly who they were, but the central point is clear.

Today we can ask whether our lives match what we say we believe. Choose one concrete action this week, such as being honest, helping someone, or forgiving, so that your faith shows in deeds and not only in words.
exp.0:14:
For those whose heart is clean, everything God has given is clean and can be received with gratitude. But for those who are defiled (stained within) and without faith, nothing is clean, because their mind and conscience are dirty.

Paul writes to Titus, who oversees the churches in Crete. Some teachers mix Jewish myths and human rules, and they focus on outward prohibitions, such as certain foods. Paul answers that the real problem is not in things but in the heart. Their deeds, he says, contradict what they profess.

For today: instead of judging others by outward rules, ask God to cleanse your heart. A sincere faith changes how you think, see, and act.
exp.0:8:
He says that the church leader must "hold fast," that is, cling firmly to the faithful word, the true teaching he received. In this way he will be able to do two things: encourage and guide others with sound doctrine, and prove wrong those who speak against it, showing their error clearly.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he left in Crete to bring order to the churches and appoint elders (called here "overseers," meaning supervisors). After describing the character the leader must have, he adds that he must also know the teaching well, because in Crete there were deceptive teachers who were leading whole households astray.

For today: it is not enough to be a good person; every believer, and especially one who guides others, needs to know the Bible so that they can respond with both firmness and kindness. Make time to read it consistently.
exp.2:5:
This verse says that God poured out the Holy Spirit on us "abundantly," that is, in great measure and without holding back. He did this through Jesus Christ, whom Paul calls "our Saviour." The phrase continues what was said before: it is the Spirit who renews us.

Paul is writing to Titus, a co-worker who was caring for the churches on Crete. He wants to remind him that salvation is not earned by good works but comes from the mercy of God. Before this verse he speaks of our past life, and afterward he explains that, having been justified by grace, we have hope of eternal life.

For today: if God gives his Spirit abundantly, you do not have to live out your faith by your own strength. Ask him for help each day, and let his grace move you to do good with gratitude, not out of mere obligation.
exp.1:6:
Paul tells Titus to show himself in everything as an example of good works. When he teaches, he must show uncorruptness, that is, purity and sincerity in what he says and does, and gravity, which means seriousness and respect for the things of God. The words "shewing" and "shewing thyself" speak of a life that can be observed.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he left in Crete to bring order to the churches. Earlier he asked him to teach older men, older women, and young people how to live. Now he reminds him that he himself must live out what he teaches, so that no one speaks evil of the gospel or of the church.

For today: before correcting or advising others, examine your own life. Choose one concrete behavior, such as honesty at work or patience at home, and practice it so that your example backs up your words.
exp.0:13:
It says that believers should not pay attention to "Jewish fables," that is, stories and tales made up but dressed in a religious appearance, nor to "commandments of men," rules invented by people. Such things turn people away from the truth. The word "heed" means to pay attention or give importance to something.

Paul is writing to Titus, who was overseeing the churches in Crete. There were teachers who mixed human teachings with the faith, and the context suggests they focused on rules about what is clean and unclean (v. 15). That is why Paul asks Titus to correct them firmly, so that the faith of everyone stays healthy.

For today: before accepting a teaching, compare it with what the Bible says. If something sounds spiritual but adds rules or stories that Jesus and the apostles did not teach, be careful and look for the truth in Scripture.
exp.0:3:
Paul greets Titus and calls him "true son in the common faith." This means that Titus was like a spiritual son to him, and that both of them shared the same faith in Christ. He then wishes him grace (God's undeserved favor), mercy (his compassion), and peace, which come from God the Father and from Jesus Christ, called our Saviour.

Paul writes this letter to Titus, one of his co-workers, whom he left on the island of Crete to set the churches in order and appoint leaders. It is not known with exactness all the details of how Titus came to faith, but the word "son" shows affection and closeness. The greeting also reminds us that Paul's message comes from God.

For today: faith unites us as a family, beyond our differences. We can encourage someone with whom we share the faith, and wish them from the heart the grace and peace of God, perhaps with a call or a message this week.
exp.2:14:
Paul closes his letter to Titus with greetings. Those who are with him send their regards, and Paul asks Titus to greet those who love them in the faith. He ends with a blessing: that grace be with all of them. The final note, about Titus as the first bishop of Crete and the letter being written from Nicopolis, is not part of the original text; it was added later by copyists, and scholars doubt its accuracy.

Paul writes to Titus, his co-worker, whom he left in Crete to put the life of the churches in order. It is a warm farewell, showing that work in the faith is never done alone, but within a network of friends and companions.

Today we can imitate this gesture: greeting, remembering, and encouraging our brothers and sisters in the faith. A simple message of affection can strengthen someone. And let us remember that everything is sustained by the grace of God.
exp.0:11:
Paul quotes a saying about the people of Crete: that they are always liars, that they are like wild beasts, and that they live thinking only about eating and not working. "Slow bellies" describes greedy, lazy people, ruled by their appetites.

Paul is writing to Titus, who oversees the churches in Crete. He speaks of false teachers who deceive and teach for profit. "One of themselves, even a prophet of their own" is commonly understood to mean a Cretan poet; many think of Epimenides, although the text does not name him. Paul is not insulting people for the sake of it. He uses this well-known saying to show why Titus must correct firmly and seek to help the people grow healthy in the faith.

Today, let us be careful not to label an entire people with prejudice. Rather, let us be honest when we correct what harms, with truth and with love, seeking to see others restored.
exp.2:2:
Paul reminds us that we Christians were also once foolish, that is, without spiritual understanding. We were rebellious and lost, slaves to disordered desires and to pleasures of every kind. We lived in malice and envy, we were hateful, and we hated one another.

Paul writes to Titus, who was leading the churches in Crete. He has just asked him to teach the believers to respect authorities, to do good, and to be kind to everyone. To motivate them, he reminds them of their own past. Then, in the following verse, he speaks of the kindness and mercy of God who saved them.

For today: when someone treats you badly or it is hard for you to be patient, remember where God rescued you from. That memory helps us treat others with humility and gentleness, not with pride.
exp.2:1:
This verse says that believers should not speak evil of anyone or be quarrelsome. They should be "gentle," that is, kind and reasonable, and show "all meekness," which means a humble and calm way of treating all people. To "speak evil" means to insult someone or harm their reputation. "Quarrelsome" people are those who look for fights.

Paul is writing to Titus, who was caring for the churches in Crete. He asks him to teach how to live in the midst of a society that is not Christian. Earlier he speaks of respecting those in authority, and then he reminds them that we all were foolish and rebellious until God showed his kindness. For that reason there is no room for pride.

For today: before criticizing or arguing, especially on social media or with someone who thinks differently, remember the patience God showed you and respond with calm and respect.
exp.2:6:
This verse says that God declares us righteous by his grace, that is, by his undeserved favor. "Justified" means that God accepts us as if we had no guilt. And so we become "heirs," people who receive an inheritance: the eternal life we hope for.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he left on the island of Crete to help organize the churches. Before this verse he reminds them that salvation did not come through our good works, but through God's mercy. Afterward he insists that those who believe should devote themselves to doing good, and to avoiding useless arguments.

For today: you do not have to earn God's love. Rest in his grace, and let that gratitude lead you to serve others with joy, not out of obligation or fear.
exp.2:3:
The verse says that God showed his kindness and love toward people when his Saviour appeared. The word "appeared" means that it became visible, that it was made known. "Toward man" means toward humanity. Here the word "love" translates a Greek expression that speaks of tender affection for human beings.

The apostle Paul is writing to Titus, who was caring for the churches of Crete. He has just asked the believers to treat everyone with gentleness, and he reminds them that they too were once foolish and rebellious. The word "But" marks the change: it was not because of their own merit, but because of God's goodness. Many understand that this appearing refers to the coming of Jesus.

Today, when someone bothers us or lets us down, let us remember how much patience God showed toward us, and respond with kindness.
exp.1:10:
This verse says that the grace of God, that is, his undeserved favor, has been revealed to all people. That grace brings salvation and is available to every kind of person. The word "appeared" means it became visible, and many understand this as referring to the coming of Jesus Christ.

Paul is writing to Titus, who was overseeing the churches in Crete. He has just given instructions to different groups, including slaves, and now gives the underlying reason: the grace of God has come even to them. For that reason, their good conduct can display the beauty of the gospel.

For today: if grace is for everyone, treat each person, regardless of their position, as someone God loves. And let that grace show in your work and in your daily dealings, with honesty and a good attitude.
exp.1:12:
This verse says that believers live looking forward to something very good: the "blessed hope," that is, a hope full of happiness. That hope is the glorious appearing of Jesus Christ, whom Paul calls "the great God and our Saviour." The word "appearing" means a manifestation, the moment when Christ will be shown to everyone. Some scholars also discuss whether the phrase refers to one person (Jesus is the great God and Saviour) or to two, but most translations support the first idea.

The apostle Paul is writing to Titus, who was overseeing the churches on the island of Crete. He wants Titus to teach people to live uprightly. For this reason, he first speaks of the grace that teaches us to turn away from wickedness, and then he reminds them that Christ gave himself for us.

For today: when you feel tired or tempted to live without direction, remember that Christ will return. That hope encourages you to live with honesty and patience each day.
exp.1:4:
This verse continues the list of what older women are to teach younger women. It asks that they be "self-controlled" (self-mastery, good sense), "pure" (chaste, faithful), careful keepers of the home, and "kind" (gentle, generous). It also speaks of being "submissive" to their own husbands, that is, respecting their place in the family. The reason given is that the word of God should not be "spoken against," that is, spoken of with contempt.

Paul is writing to Titus, whom he left in Crete to set the churches in order. He wants the daily lives of believers to support the message of the gospel before a society that was watching them. Some understand the "submission" in terms of the culture of that time; others see it as a lasting principle. Christians explain it in different ways.

Today we can ask ourselves: does the way I treat my family and manage my home make what I say about God believable? Choose one concrete act of patience or service in your home today.
exp.0:0:
Paul presents himself as a "servant of God," meaning someone who belongs to God and obeys him, and as an "apostle of Jesus Christ," someone sent with authority by Christ. He says his work is "according to the faith of God's elect," that is, to awaken and strengthen the faith of those whom God has called. He also seeks "the acknowledging of the truth which is after godliness": knowing the truth that leads to living with reverence and obedience toward God.

Paul writes this letter to Titus, his co-worker, whom he left on the island of Crete to set the churches in order. Before giving instructions, Paul reminds them where his authority comes from: God sent him. Some scholars debate details about the date of the letter, but they present it as coming from Paul.

For today: biblical truth is not just information, but should transform the way we live. Today you can ask yourself: "Does what I know about God show in my conduct?"
exp.2:10:
The divisive person, after being corrected again and again and still staying the same, is clearly "subverted," that is, twisted or turned off the right path. He also "sins," because he insists on the error. And he is "condemned by his own judgment": his own conduct shows him to be guilty, since he knows he was warned and still did not want to change.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he left in charge of the churches in Crete. He asks him to avoid useless arguments about genealogies and the law, and to warn the person who causes divisions. If after two warnings there is no change, Titus should keep away from him. Then Paul moves on to practical matters, such as travel plans and help for other co-workers.

For today: correct with humility and patience, but do not spend your strength on endless fights. If someone rejects the advice again and again, keep your distance peacefully and continue serving.
exp.0:12:
Paul says that what the Cretan poet said about his own people is true in this case. So he asks Titus to correct them firmly. Correcting them with seriousness, without softening the message, is what the rebuke is meant to do. The goal is that they be sound in the faith, that is, that they live a firm faith free of error.

Paul writes to Titus, who is in Crete helping to organize the churches. There were false teachers who deceived whole families for money. Paul quotes a Cretan poet, whose name is not known for certain; he is only described as a prophet of their own people. The sharpness seeks to heal, not to humiliate.

For today: if you must correct someone in the church or in your family, do it with clarity and truth, but with the desire that the person be restored. Correct in order to heal, not to win an argument.
exp.1:8:
He says that Titus should encourage servants to submit to their masters, to try to please them in everything, and not to be argumentative, that is, not to answer back with insolence or to dispute stubbornly. "Servants" here means slaves or people who worked under the authority of another.

Paul writes to Titus, who was left in charge of the churches on Crete. He wants the lives of believers to be so good that no one can speak badly of the gospel. Paul does not say here that slavery is good; he gives instructions for living with a witness within the reality of that time. The following verse explains the purpose: to adorn the teaching of God.

For today: at work, try to do your labor with honesty, respect and a good attitude, even when something is not to your liking. You can express your disagreements calmly, without mockery or rebellion, so that your conduct speaks well of Christ.
exp.2:9:
It says that the person who is a "heretic" must be rejected, but only after being warned again and again. "Heretic" here does not refer to someone who simply thinks differently on a minor matter, but to the one who causes divisions and stubbornly persists in them. "Rejected" means to turn away from, not to give room to. "Admonition" means a warning or correction given clearly.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he left in charge of the churches in Crete. He has just asked him to avoid foolish arguments and quarrels about the law. Now he explains what to do with someone who insists on dividing: first warn him, and if he does not listen, turn away from him. The next verse says that such a person condemns himself by his stubbornness.

For today: when someone divides people with their arguments, correct them with patience and love, more than once. If they refuse to listen, do not spend your strength on quarrels; guard the peace of the church.
exp.1:9:
This verse says that servants should not "pilfer" from their masters, that is, they should not steal or deceive them in small things. Instead, they should show "all good fidelity," meaning complete and trustworthy faithfulness. In this way they "adorn" the teaching about God, that is, they make it look beautiful and attractive to others.

Paul is writing to Titus, who was overseeing the churches in Crete. At that time there were many servants or slaves, and Paul wants their honest conduct to give the opposition nothing bad to say. What follows explains that the grace of God teaches us to live in the right way.

Today we can apply this at work: being honest with our time, our money, and our tasks, even when no one is watching. Our daily integrity can lead others to see the gospel as something good and believable.
exp.0:9:
This verse says that in Crete there were many people who were rebellious, who spoke empty things, and who deceived people's hearts. Paul points especially to those "of the circumcision," that is, to believers of Jewish background who insisted on practices of the law.

Paul writes to Titus, whom he left in Crete to put the churches in order. After asking that the leaders be upright and firm in sound teaching, he explains why this is so necessary: there were teachers who caused division and taught for profit. Not all of that group were like this; Paul is speaking of those who were.

For today: do not let yourself be carried along by whoever sounds persuasive. Compare what you hear with the Bible, and make sure that whoever teaches lives with integrity and does not seek his own gain.
exp.2:8:
Paul tells Titus to stay away from foolish arguments, from long lists of ancestors, from quarrels, and from debates about the law. He says that all of this brings nothing good and leads nowhere.

Paul is writing to Titus, his co-worker, who was guiding the churches in Crete. Just before this, he reminded readers that we are saved by grace and that this faith should produce good works. For that reason, fruitless arguments distract from what matters. It is not known precisely which genealogies they were debating, but they seem to have been Jewish debates about the law and about origins.

For today: before getting into an argument, ask yourself whether it helps someone know Christ better or do good. If it only creates conflict and pride, leave it alone and spend your time serving others.
exp.0:2:
He says that God, at the time He chose, made known His word through preaching. Paul explains that this task was entrusted to him by the command of God, whom he calls "our Savior."

Paul writes to Titus, his co-worker, who is on the island of Crete. At the beginning of the letter, Paul reminds him that God promised eternal life before time began and has now revealed it. With this he affirms that his authority does not come from himself but from God, since Titus was to appoint elders in the churches.

God continues to speak through the preaching of His word. We can listen with respect, and if God has entrusted us with teaching others, we should do so with humility and faithfulness, without inventing anything of our own.
exp.2:7:
This is a trustworthy saying, and Paul wants Titus to insist on these things firmly. The goal is that those who believe in God should be careful to devote themselves to good works, that is, make an effort to direct their lives toward doing good. To affirm these things means to teach them with conviction. These things are good and profitable for everyone.

Paul writes to Titus, who oversees the churches in Crete. He has just explained that God saved us by his grace, not by our own merits. Now he clarifies that this salvation should produce a life of good works. Then he warns against useless arguments that distract from what is important.

For today: Since God helped us without our deserving it, this week look for a concrete way to do good for someone, such as helping a neighbor or visiting a sick person, and do it with gratitude, not to earn salvation.
exp.1:13:
This verse says that Jesus Christ gave himself for us, that is, he gave his life on the cross. He did it to rescue us by paying a price, and so to free us from all wickedness, that is, from all evil and crooked living. He also meant to cleanse for himself a people who belong to him, and to make them eager and devoted to doing good works.

Paul is writing to Titus, whom he left in charge of the church on the island of Crete. Before this verse, he explains that the grace of God teaches us to turn away from ungodliness and to live with self-control, righteousness, and devotion. Here he gives the deeper reason: Christ gave himself to transform us. Then he asks Titus to teach this with authority.

For today: salvation is not only forgiveness, it also leads us into a new life. Today you can choose one concrete act of kindness, such as helping a neighbor or serving in your church, as a response of gratitude to Christ.

sum.1: Paul tells Titus to teach healthy living to each group: older men, older women, younger people, and slaves, so that they live with self-control, good example, and integrity. The reason is that God's grace has brought salvation, teaches us to turn away from ungodliness, and Jesus Christ gave himself to cleanse a people eager to do good works.
sum.2: Paul tells Titus to teach believers to respect those in authority, to be gentle, and to do what is good. He reminds them that God saved them through his mercy and not because of their works, and so they should live out lives of good deeds. He also advises Titus to avoid pointless arguments, and he closes with instructions and greetings.
sum.0: Paul reminds Titus that he left him in Crete to put the church in order and to appoint elders whose lives are blameless, who are faithful in their households and firm in sound teaching. He also warns him about deceptive teachers who are in it for money, and asks Titus to rebuke them firmly. He says that those who claim to know God but deny him by their actions are unfit for doing any good.
